problems.title: Problem 1: Intel Xeon multi-level cache hierarchy (Questions A-D)
problems.anchor_text: Problem 1: (21 points) -- One possible organization of the memory hierarchy on an Intel Xeon chip is:
subparts: A (3 pts): three True/False statements about the cache hierarchy
B (6 pts): tag/index/offset split of a 64-bit physical address for the 4-way 512KB L2
C (10 pts): maximum initial main memory access time in ns for AMAT <= 4 CCs
D (2 pts): AMAT in CCs when the processor-memory bus widens to 32 Bytes
problems.grouped_with_reason: A, B, C and D all sit on top of one shared machine description (2.0 GHz, 128-Byte blocks, L1/L2/L3 hit times of 1/10/50 CCs, 16-Byte bus, +10 CCs per additional transfer) that is stated once before Question A and never repeated. D explicitly says 'Assuming the same local miss rates in Question C' and reuses the multi-level AMAT expression and the maximum initial memory access time that C solves for, so D is unanswerable without C's result. Splitting these would make two workers re-derive the same hierarchy model and risk them disagreeing on the transfer-count convention.

problems.title: Problem 2: Virtual memory address split and page table sizing (Questions A-C)
problems.anchor_text: Problem 2: (10 points) -- Consider the following parameters of a virtual memory system:
subparts: A (2 pts): fill Table 2 -- page offset bits, VPN bits, total bits
B (4 pts): number of PTEs and physical memory needed to store the page table
C (4 pts): pros and cons of increasing the page size (at least 1 each)
problems.grouped_with_reason: All three questions read from one shared Table 1 (30-bit virtual address, 2 GB physical memory, 64 KB page size, 4-Byte PTE). B's entry count is exactly 2^(VPN bits) computed in A, so B is a direct continuation of A. C is the qualitative discussion of the same parameter A and B quantify. A single worker keeps the page-size arithmetic consistent across all three.

problems.title: Problem 3: Way-prediction on an L1 instruction cache (Questions A-B)
problems.anchor_text: Problem 3: (8 points) -- We are trying to deploy the way-prediction technique on an L1 instruction cache.
subparts: A (2 pts): best-case and worst-case cache access time in ns with way-prediction enabled
B (6 pts): minimum prediction accuracy for the way-predicting cache to cut AMAT by at least 5%
problems.grouped_with_reason: One shared cache configuration (4-way, 64-Byte blocks, 256 KB, 1.1 ns baseline access, 1% miss rate, 50 ns miss penalty; 1 ns on a correct way prediction, 1.1 ns additional on a wrong one). B's AMAT expression is built directly out of the best-case and worst-case access times that A asks for, so answering B requires A's numbers.

problems.title: Problem 4: Critical-word first and early restart (Questions A-C)
problems.anchor_text: Problem 4: (16 points) -- Consider applying critical-word first and early restart techniques to reduce miss penalty in a system with L1 and L2 caches.
subparts: A (8 pts): average CCs to service an L2 miss under three schemes (neither / early restart only / both)
B (4 pts): fill two integer blanks in the L1 analysis paragraph
C (4 pts): is critical-word first / early restart more important for L1 or L2, and why
problems.grouped_with_reason: Question B opens with 'For this question, ignore Question A', which decouples B's arithmetic from A's -- but Question C then says 'You may refer to your observations while solving Questions A and B', so C is a comparison that consumes the numeric results of BOTH A and B. Splitting A from B would leave whichever worker got C without half its evidence, and the shared framing (a word is 8 Bytes wide; the meaning of 'neither / early restart only / both') is stated once at the top of the problem.
